prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the 3D geometry of a living room corner, showing a television on a stand about 2.5 to 3 metres straight ahead against the left wall, flanked by a taller shelving unit about 2 metres away on the left (1 metre left of the TV) and a smaller shelf about 3.5 metres away in the dark back corner (1 metre right of the TV). Closer to the camera wearer, a round ottoman at the bottom-left and a low coffee table along the right wall sit roughly 1 to 1.5 metres away, with toy blocks on the floor between them at about 1.5 metres. In frames 1 to 4 the viewpoint stays steady before panning right in frame 5, where a person in blue and a raised left hand enter the lower-right foreground at less than 0.5 metres—well within arm's reach of the camera wearer and each other, partially occluding the sofa and coffee table behind them—while the left shelf moves out of view. The person on the far right is heavily cropped at the frame edge and appears oriented sideways toward the left (toward the TV or camera wearer) rather than facing directly into the lens. This map clarifies the continuous distance gradient along the right wall, floor, and recessed ceiling and cleanly separates the sub-metre foreground person and sofa from the 2-to-3-metre background furniture more distinctly than RGB alone, though it is unreliable on the wall clock (which vanishes into the flat wall plane) and inside the open shelving cubbies where depth boundaries blur.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates discrete objects in the room across the 5-frame rightward pan, consistently detecting the television screen (2.5 to 3 metres ahead), the potted plant resting on the top-left corner of the left shelf (about 2 metres away and slightly above the TV), the circular clock mounted on the wall above the TV (except in frames 3 and 5), and the low table on the right at 1 to 1.5 metres. In frame 5, as the camera turns right, it segments the partially visible person in blue and the adjacent foreground hand/arm in the bottom-right corner within 0.5 metres (within arm's reach of the camera wearer and each other), where the foreground masks overlap and partially occlude the green table mask behind them. While segmentation provides crisp 2D object boundaries for the TV, plant, and table that separate them from cluttered surroundings, it is highly unreliable for semantic and spatial scene understanding here. It completely misses the shelving units, floor toys, ottoman, and sofa, inconsistently labels the right-side coffee table as a 'bed' in frame 1, 'dining table' in frames 2, 4, and 5, and omits it in frame 3, and misclassifies the bowl of fruit on that table as 'pizza' in frame 4. Furthermore, it falsely segments 2D cartoon characters and an eagle displayed on the flat TV screen (2.5 to 3 metres away) as real 'person' instances in frames 2 through 5, creating false-positive subjects that appear to face the room.
descriptions.pose: The body/hand skeleton map is completely blank across frames 1 to 4, confirming that no real people are visible in the room during the initial stationary view toward the television and shelves 2 to 3.5 metres away. In frame 5, as the camera wearer turns rightward, a single yellow upper-body/arm skeletal segment appears in the bottom-right corner, corresponding to the person in a blue shirt positioned within 0.5 metres (arm's reach) of the camera wearer and roughly 1.5 metres in front of the coffee table. The diagonal orientation of this skeletal link from the right edge down toward the lower-right indicates the person's torso and arm are angled leftward across the lower foreground rather than facing squarely into the camera, with most of their body and head cropped out of the right frame boundary. Unlike the segmentation map, the pose estimator usefully filters out the 2D cartoon figures on the TV screen 2.5 to 3 metres away and isolates only the real foreground person in frame 5. However, the map is largely unreliable in frame 5 because heavy edge truncation and close proximity cause it to miss the person's full torso and head orientation, and it completely fails to render a magenta hand skeleton for the open hand clearly visible within arm's reach at the bottom-right next to the person.
